title: Security Principles
description: Foundational security concepts including the CIA Triad, authentication, authorization, non-repudiation, risk management, governance, controls, and professional ethics.

topics.title: Cybersecurity Concepts (CIA Triad, AAA, Non-Repudiation, Privacy)
topics.content:
The CIA Triad represents the three core principles of information security: Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability. These principles form the foundation upon which all security programs and controls are built.

Confidentiality ensures that information is accessible only to those authorized to access it. This is achieved through mechanisms such as encryption, access controls, and data classification. A breach of confidentiality occurs when unauthorized individuals gain access to sensitive data, whether through hacking, social engineering, or improper data handling.

Integrity ensures that data remains accurate, complete, and unaltered except by authorized parties through authorized mechanisms. Integrity controls include hashing algorithms, digital signatures, version control systems, and input validation. When integrity is compromised, organizations cannot trust the accuracy of their data, leading to flawed decision-making and potential regulatory violations.

Availability ensures that information and systems are accessible to authorized users when needed. This is maintained through redundancy, fault tolerance, proper capacity planning, and disaster recovery procedures. Denial-of-service attacks, hardware failures, and natural disasters are common threats to availability.

Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) provide the framework for tracking and controlling user access. Authentication verifies identity, authorization determines permissions, and accounting tracks resource consumption and user actions for auditing purposes.

Non-repudiation is the assurance that a party in a communication or transaction cannot deny the authenticity of their signature or the sending of a message. Digital signatures are the primary mechanism for achieving non-repudiation, providing proof of origin and data integrity.

Privacy focuses on the proper handling, processing, and protection of personally identifiable information (PII) in compliance with relevant regulations.

topics.title: Risk Management Concepts
topics.content:
Risk management is the systematic process of identifying, assessing, and mitigating risks to an organization's information assets. It involves understanding the relationship between threats, vulnerabilities, and the potential impact of security incidents.

A threat is any potential event or action that could cause harm to an asset. A vulnerability is a weakness in a system, process, or control that could be exploited by a threat. Risk is the likelihood that a threat will exploit a vulnerability and the resulting impact on the organization. The formula is often expressed as: Risk = Threat x Vulnerability x Impact.

Quantitative risk analysis assigns numerical values to risk components. Key formulas include: Single Loss Expectancy (SLE) = Asset Value x Exposure Factor; Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO) represents how often a loss is expected per year; and Annualized Loss Expectancy (ALE) = SLE x ARO. Qualitative risk analysis uses subjective ratings such as high, medium, and low to categorize risks.

Risk treatment options include risk mitigation (implementing controls to reduce risk), risk acceptance (acknowledging and accepting the risk), risk avoidance (eliminating the activity that creates risk), and risk transfer (shifting risk to a third party, such as through insurance or outsourcing).

topics.title: Governance Concepts, Laws, and Regulations
topics.content: Governance concepts encompass the overarching rules, laws, regulations, and frameworks that direct how an organization manages its security posture. Regulations and laws dictate mandatory compliance standards based on industry and geographic jurisdiction. Frameworks and guidelines (such as ISO standards and Center for Internet Security benchmarks) provide structured methodologies for establishing security controls. Policies are high-level mandatory directives set by management, standards specify mandatory requirements, and procedures provide step-by-step implementation instructions.

topics.title: Cybersecurity Controls
topics.content:
Cybersecurity controls are safeguards or countermeasures implemented to avoid, detect, counteract, or minimize security risks. They are categorized into three main types:

Technical Controls (Logical controls) use hardware, software, and firmware mechanisms to protect systems and data (e.g., firewalls, encryption, identification systems, and access control lists).

Administrative Controls (Management controls) consist of policies, procedures, guidelines, and organizational practices that direct personnel behavior and operational security.

Physical Controls protect the physical environment, facilities, equipment, and assets through barriers, security guards, mantraps, and environmental sensors.

topics.title: Professional and Ethical Conduct
topics.content: Maintaining professional and ethical conduct is essential for cybersecurity practitioners. The ISC2 Code of Ethics provides core canons that guide professional behavior, emphasizing the protection of society, the commonwealth, and the infrastructure. Practitioners must act honorably, honestly, responsibly, and legally, providing diligent and competent service to principals. Due care and due diligence represent the legal and practical standards of behavior: due care is the practice of acting responsibly and taking reasonable steps to protect assets (doing what is right), while due diligence is the continuous effort and investigation to ensure that risks are managed and controls are maintained (doing your homework).

title: Security Governance
description: Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) planning, business continuity, disaster recovery, security awareness, and measuring cybersecurity effectiveness.

topics.title: Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) Planning
topics.content: Planning Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) ensures that an organization's security strategy aligns with business goals while meeting legal and regulatory requirements. The purpose and importance of GRC lie in establishing clear oversight, reducing operational friction, and providing structured frameworks and tools to manage risk cohesively across the enterprise.

topics.title: Redundancy, Business Continuity, and Disaster Recovery
topics.content:
Redundancy ensures high availability and fault tolerance through duplicate systems or data paths. Business Continuity (BC) and Disaster Recovery (DR) are critical components of operational resilience.

Business Continuity Planning (BCP) is the process of creating systems of prevention and recovery to deal with potential threats, ensuring critical business functions continue during a disruption. The Business Impact Analysis (BIA) identifies critical functions and metrics such as Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD). Plans are validated through exercises such as tabletop exercises and walkthroughs.

Disaster Recovery (DR) targets the technical recovery of IT infrastructure and data using metrics like Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO), alongside alternate processing sites such as hot, warm, and cold sites.

topics.title: Security Awareness and Culture
topics.content: Security awareness programs foster an organizational culture that prioritizes security, driven by active security leadership and employee engagement. Core concepts include training personnel to recognize social engineering tactics, practice robust password management, and identify phishing attempts. A strong security culture ensures employees act as the first line of defense against cyber threats.

topics.title: Measuring Cybersecurity Effectiveness
topics.content: Measuring cybersecurity effectiveness involves tracking performance and risk levels using key metrics and Key Risk Indicators (KRIs). Organizations aggregate this data into dashboards, scorecards, and reports to communicate security posture to executive leadership and make informed strategic adjustments.

title: Identity And Access Management (IAM) Concepts
description: Identity lifecycle management, logical access controls, access control models, least privilege, and separation of duties.

topics.title: Identity Lifecycle Management
topics.content:
Identity lifecycle management governs digital identities from creation to termination across enterprise systems. It includes role definition, provisioning accounts securely, regular access reviews, and deprovisioning accounts promptly when personnel leave or change roles. Specialized frameworks and tools centralize directory services and identity governance.

Logical access controls enforce authorization policies by restricting access to systems and networks. Single Sign-On (SSO), Identity Management systems, and Privileged Access Management (PAM) are core components of logical access control.

topics.title: Logical Access Control Principles and Models
topics.content:
Logical access controls rely on core security principles and established architectural models to protect sensitive resources.

The Principle of Least Privilege (POLP) dictates that users and processes should be granted only the minimum permissions necessary to perform their tasks. Separation of Duties (SOD) ensures that critical tasks are divided among multiple individuals, preventing any single person from holding complete control over a sensitive process.

Access control models define rules for granting or denying access:
- Discretionary Access Control (DAC) allows resource owners to manage permissions, though it is flexible, it is vulnerable to unauthorized sharing.
- Mandatory Access Control (MAC) enforces strict access based on security labels and clearance levels, common in high-security environments.
- Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) assigns permissions to organizational roles rather than individuals, streamlining management and supporting least privilege.

title: Networking and Cloud Security Concepts
description: Network architecture, OSI and TCP/IP models, firewalls, wireless, embedded systems, IoT, network segmentation, defense in depth, zero trust, and cloud security.

topics.title: Network Security Concepts and Protocols
topics.content:
Network security relies on standardized communication models and robust perimeter defenses. The OSI model (seven layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application) and the TCP/IP model provide the conceptual framework for data transmission. Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) and Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) handle logical addressing. Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) establish secure, encrypted communication tunnels over public networks.

Firewalls inspect traffic based on ports, protocols, and application awareness to control network boundaries. Wireless security (covering Wi-Fi protocols and Bluetooth) requires robust encryption and authentication to prevent unauthorized airwave interception. Embedded systems (such as Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA)) and Internet of Things (IoT) devices introduce specialized security challenges due to resource constraints and critical operational roles.

topics.title: Network Security Architecture
topics.content:
Network security architecture implements layered defenses to protect infrastructure from sophisticated threats. Network segmentation divides networks into isolated zones using firewall rules, Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs), and micro-segmentation to restrict lateral movement by attackers.

Defense in Depth utilizes multiple layers of security controls so that the failure of any single safeguard does not compromise the entire environment. Zero Trust (ZT) shifts the security paradigm from perimeter-based trust to continuous verification, operating under the principle of "never trust, always verify" for every user and device attempting access.

topics.title: Cloud Security Concepts and Architecture
topics.content:
Cloud computing introduces specific characteristics, service models, and shared responsibility frameworks that redefine traditional security architectures.

Core characteristics include broad network access, rapid elasticity, measured service, on-demand self-service, and resource pooling.

Service models define the division of capabilities: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Software as a Service (SaaS).

Deployment models include public, private, hybrid, and community clouds.

The Shared Security Model outlines the division of security responsibilities between the cloud service provider (CSP) and the customer, varying depending on whether the model is IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS.

title: Security Operations and Incident Response
description: Data security, encryption, security operations, logging, monitoring, threat intelligence, incident response, asset protection, and security testing.

topics.title: Data Security and Cryptography
topics.content:
Data security encompasses proper handling and cryptographic protection throughout the data lifecycle. Data handling practices include classification, labeling, masking, and sanitization to protect information at rest, in transit, and in use.

Encryption technologies protect data confidentiality and integrity. Symmetric encryption uses a single shared key for encryption and decryption, while asymmetric encryption utilizes public-private key pairs. Hashing provides mathematical one-way checksums to verify data integrity. Emerging quantum-resistant cryptography aims to secure data against future quantum computing decryption threats.

topics.title: Security Operations, Threat Intelligence, and Triage
topics.content: Security operations involve continuous monitoring and defense of organizational assets. Logging and monitoring security events using SIEM platforms provide visibility into anomalous behavior. Security event triage involves evaluating incident use cases, prioritizing alerts, and correlating data streams. Understanding threat actors (their types, motivations, and capabilities) alongside Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) and standardized threat frameworks helps security teams anticipate and counteract attacks.

topics.title: Incident Response (IR)
topics.content: Incident Response (IR) provides a structured approach for managing security breaches. Effective IR requires implementing a data handling policy that aligns with the Incident Response Plan (IRP). Organizations validate their readiness through Incident Response exercises, including testing and tabletop simulations, to ensure seamless execution during actual cyber incidents.

topics.title: Asset Protection and Configuration Management
topics.content: Asset protection involves managing hardware, software, and data assets throughout their operational lifecycle. Asset lifecycle management includes tracking End Of Life (EOL) software and unsupported devices to prevent unpatched vulnerabilities. Configuration and change management ensure that modifications to systems are strictly controlled, documented, and reviewed to prevent unauthorized configuration drift.

topics.title: Security Testing
topics.content: Security testing validates the effectiveness of defensive controls and identifies hidden vulnerabilities. Security readiness testing includes blue teaming (defense), red teaming (offensive simulation), and purple teaming (collaborative integration). Application testing encompasses vulnerability scanning, static analysis, dynamic analysis, and threat modeling. Physical penetration testing evaluates physical security controls through methods such as social engineering, phishing, tailgating, and impersonation.
